claims.text: ML interatomic potentials trained on ab initio data can accurately and efficiently determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family when combined with two-phase molecular dynamics and free-energy integration.
The targeted solid phases are substitutionally disordered, multi-principal-element random solid solutions.
Representative DFT datasets for selected alloy systems can be used to develop neural-network or Gaussian-approximation interatomic potentials.
Two-phase coexistence simulations using the ML potentials can determine melting temperatures.
Thermodynamic integration can extract enthalpy, entropy, and volume changes at melting.
The relevant melting regime for the targeted alloys is typically 1000–2000 K, depending on alloy chemistry.
The ML potentials capture local chemical disorder and fluctuations in bonding environments associated with the solid-to-liquid transition.
Capturing disorder-dependent bonding environments enables accurate resolution of atomic interactions in both solid and liquid phases.
Replacing ab initio molecular dynamics with ML-driven potentials preserves near-DFT accuracy.
Replacing ab initio molecular dynamics with ML-driven potentials makes high-throughput two-phase simulations feasible.
Dual-phase molecular dynamics directly observes melting transitions.
The approach will predict melting temperatures within approximately ±10 K of experimental values.
The approach will predict fusion enthalpy and entropy within approximately ±5% of experimental values.
The approach will predict volume change at melting within 2–3% accuracy.
The approach will reliably produce liquid-phase free-energy curves and related thermodynamic properties.
Conventional CALPHAD models and empirical extrapolations typically assume defect-free crystals or idealized behavior.
Conventional CALPHAD models and empirical extrapolations struggle with the chemical disorder and complexity of high-entropy alloys.
Reliable application is limited to alloy chemistries adequately represented by the ML potential's training set.
Performance may degrade for rare-earth-containing alloys, highly nonideal mixtures, or other compositions far outside the training regime.
Long-timescale kinetic effects may not be fully captured in glass-forming or sluggish systems.
